body.text: Japan and China increasingly view each other through interconnected theatres of strategic risk, creating a security dynamic in which each side’s response to insecurity reinforces the other’s perception of threat

The recently released 2026 Defence of Japan Pamphlet and Tsinghua University’s 2026 Overall Risk Landscape offer a revealing mirror image of how Japan and China increasingly view one another. Japan’s White Paper carries official endorsement, whereas the report by Tsinghua University’s Center for International Studies and Strategy (CISS) — which collates the views of many strategists — provides clues to how China appraises strategic risks.

The two assessments are strikingly reciprocal, though they do not assign each other identical strategic roles. Tokyo and Beijing appear caught in a mutually reinforcing security spiral. Japan increasingly reads China as the organising variable of its security environment, while China increasingly reads Japan not as an isolated regional rival but as a forward component of a wider US-led strategic architecture. Where Japan’s White Paper speaks of bolstering deterrence and response capabilities through bilateral and multilateral allies and partners, China perceives systematic containment. The result is a growing convergence in threat perception: each country sees the other as both an immediate security concern and an enabler of a larger, adverse strategic environment, and the two contest how developments in the Taiwan Strait, the East China Sea, and the wider Western Pacific are connected.

Where Japan’s White Paper speaks of bolstering deterrence and response capabilities through bilateral and multilateral allies and partners, China perceives systematic containment. The result is a growing convergence in threat perception: each country sees the other as both an immediate security concern and an enabler of a larger, adverse strategic environment.

The Japanese document describes China as an “unprecedented and the greatest strategic challenge” and links its military expansion to developments across the East China Sea, Taiwan, and the Western Pacific, as well as to China-Russia cooperation. What stands out in the Japanese assessment is the extent to which China has become the connective tissue of Tokyo’s security outlook. Taiwan, the East China Sea, the South China Sea, alliance management, defence-industrial policy, and even the transformation of Japan’s defence capabilities increasingly derive their urgency from Chinese military power. This is a significant shift from treating China as one among several regional contingencies. North Korea remains an acute and immediate threat, and Russia poses its own challenges, but China is presented as the actor whose expanding capabilities can affect multiple theatres simultaneously. The implication is that Japan no longer sees its security environment as compartmentalised: a contingency in one maritime space can quickly generate consequences in another.

Taiwan best illustrates this changing geography of Japanese threat perception. Tokyo’s concern is no longer confined to whether conflict might occur across the Strait, but increasingly extends to the operational consequences of a Taiwan contingency for Japan’s southwestern islands, sea lanes, and alliance commitments. The Japanese paper notes China’s intensified military activities around Taiwan, its efforts to create a fait accompli through PLA operations, and the possibility of a grey-zone blockade involving the China Coast Guard. Japan thus increasingly views Taiwan not simply as a distant political dispute but as a contingency that could transform the strategic environment immediately adjacent to Japanese territory.

This is precisely where the Tsinghua report offers a parallel image. Taiwan is identified as China’s foremost external security risk, but, in its framing, the danger stems from the convergence of political developments in Taiwan, US engagement, and Japan’s deepening involvement. More broadly, the report warns of an unprecedented “three-seas linkage” connecting the East China Sea, the Taiwan Strait, and the South China Sea. Japan’s perceived growing intent to intervene in Taiwan is therefore seen not as an isolated bilateral problem but as part of a wider effort to generate simultaneous pressure along China’s periphery. The strategic irony is clear: Japan sees Chinese pressure around Taiwan as bringing the threat closer to Japan, while China sees Japanese involvement in Taiwan as carrying the threat to its own doorstep.

The East China Sea is where these competing strategic maps overlap most directly. For Japan, Chinese activities around the Senkaku Islands are evidence of persistent attempts to alter the status quo through coercion. The Japanese paper places these activities within China’s broader expansion from the East China Sea into the Western Pacific. For Beijing, however, the East China Sea is increasingly inseparable from the Taiwan question. The Tsinghua report’s “three-seas” framework effectively treats the East China Sea as part of a connected maritime frontier rather than a separate sovereignty dispute. Meanwhile, the China Coast Guard’s presence around the Senkaku/Diaoyu Islands has become steadily more persistent: according to the chief of the China Coast Guard, Chinese vessels operated in the surrounding contiguous zone on 357 days in 2025.

Japan figures prominently in China’s security-risk calculus, with the bilateral relationship, perceived to be at its lowest ebb, having moved from “manageable friction” to “structural competition”. Tensions flared in November 2025 after Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s assertion that a Taiwan contingency involving the use of force could constitute a “survival-threatening situation” for Japan, one in which Tokyo could exercise the right of collective self-defence under its 2015 security legislation. Takaichi’s remark was prompted by a parliamentary question and did not form part of an official government statement. The Chinese government has described Taiwan as a “core interest”, underscoring its importance to China’s sovereignty and territorial integrity. Beijing holds the right-wing orientation of Takaichi’s administration responsible, accusing it of seeking to revive Japanese militarism. Chinese scholars such as Wu Jinan, a senior researcher at the Shanghai Institute for International Studies, have argued that Taiwan holds sentimental value in the “strategic calculations” of Japan’s conservatives, who regard it as part of their sphere of influence.

The Tsinghua report further foresees risks arising from an escalation of the dispute over the Diaoyu/Senkaku Islands and adjacent maritime spaces, deployments of US missiles, and the possibility of a conflagration following a collision involving aircraft or ships. Indeed, China has repeatedly conducted “law-enforcement patrolling” in the waters east of Taiwan since Japan and the Philippines announced that they intended to demarcate the maritime boundary between their exclusive economic zones (EEZs) and continental shelves. Beijing has asserted its right to patrol the area to protect the rights of Chinese fisherfolk and national sovereignty. It is in this context that the risk flagged in the Tsinghua report—the linkage of the three seas and the resulting interconnectedness of the maritime theatres—becomes tangible. What Tokyo and Manila see as a bilateral maritime delimitation, Beijing reads as a wider alignment between the two countries on the question of Taiwan’s sovereignty.

The Japanese White Paper observes that rivalry and competition between states have blurred the line between security and the economy, making it imperative to strengthen economic-security measures by building supply-chain resilience and safeguarding advanced technologies. The Tsinghua report similarly perceives an increasing entanglement of economics and security, and foresees further technology curbs that aim to systemically contain China. Yet it is China that has used supply chains as a lever: its Ministry of Commerce has restricted rare-earth exports to Japan, justifying the move as retaliation for Takaichi’s comments on Taiwan. Since Beijing itself treats supply chains as an instrument of leverage, the Tsinghua report in effect projects some of its own fears onto the future actions of other nations.

The deeper problem is that each country increasingly reads the other’s actions as demanding an immediate strategic response. Tokyo sees a China whose military, maritime, and grey-zone activities are steadily eroding the boundaries between separate contingencies. Beijing sees a Japan whose military transformation and posture on Taiwan are embedding it more deeply within a regional containment architecture. The danger lies in this reciprocal consolidation of threat perception. Once Taiwan and the East China Sea cease to be separate disputes and become mutually reinforcing theatres, pressure in one can be used to signal resolve in the other. Rivalry then turns self-referential: each side’s effort to manage its own insecurity becomes further evidence of hostile intent in the eyes of the other.

There are implications for New Delhi too. Against the backdrop of a protracted border standoff in recent years, the Tsinghua report mentions India in the context of the possibility of its using “terrorist organizations” against China. It also voices concern about the threat of terrorism to Beijing’s investments in the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC), which runs through territory under Pakistan’s occupation.

It is worth noting in this connection that the Chinese readout of the meeting between Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi quotes India as assuring China that there has been no change in its policies on Taiwan and Tibet, and that Indian territory would not be used for “anti-China” activities, even though the Indian readout mentioned neither assurance. Historically, Beijing has harboured deep suspicions of the Dalai Lama and has accused the “Dalai Clique” of activities aimed at undermining Chinese sovereignty and territorial integrity. China has objected to what it perceives as support for the Tibetan cause among India’s political class, especially on the question of the Dalai Lama’s succession. It has asserted that the matter of the religious leader’s reincarnation is its internal affair. Beijing will therefore watch closely where New Delhi stands on the succession issue.

Takaichi visited India in July, and Beijing’s strategists have assessed that the trip was meant to help Japan build another front against China. The India-Japan relationship will therefore also be on China’s radar. India may seem peripheral to China’s threat calculus, but it is not exempt from it. Beijing sees New Delhi in two ways: as a strategic partner of states it regards as hostile to its interests, and as a node in a wider strategic geography where China’s economic interests and geopolitical vulnerabilities intersect.
Kalpit A. Mankikar is a Fellow with the Strategic Studies Programme at the Observer Research Foundation.
